In mathematics and physics, '''deformation quantization''' roughly amounts to finding a ([[Quantum algebra|quantum]]) algebra whose classical limit is a given (classical) algebra such as a [[Lie algebra]] or a [[Poisson algebra]].

== In physics ==
Intuitively, a [[Deformation theory|deformation]] of a mathematical object is a family of the same kind of objects that depend on some parameter(s). 
Here, it provides rules for how to deform the "classical" commutative algebra of [[observable]]s to a quantum non-commutative algebra of observables.

The basic setup in deformation  theory is to start with an algebraic structure (say a [[Lie algebra]]) and ask: Does there exist a one or more parameter(s) family of ''similar'' structures, such that for an initial value of the parameter(s) one has the same structure (Lie algebra) one started with? (The oldest illustration of this may be the realization of [[Eratosthenes]] in the ancient world that a flat Earth was deformable to a spherical Earth, with deformation parameter 1/''R''<sub>⊕</sub>.) E.g., one may define a [[Noncommutative geometry|noncommutative torus]] as a deformation quantization through  a  <small>★</small>-product to implicitly address all convergence subtleties (usually not addressed in formal deformation quantization). Insofar as the algebra of functions on a space determines the geometry of that space, the study of the star product leads to the study of a [[non-commutative geometry]] deformation of that space.

In the context of the above flat phase-space example, the star product ([[Moyal product]], actually introduced by [[Hilbrand_J._Groenewold|Groenewold]] in 1946), <small>★</small><sub>''ħ''</sub>, of a pair of functions in  {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>, ''f''<sub>2</sub> ∈ ''C''<sup>∞</sup>(ℜ<sup>2</sup>)}}, is specified by
: <math>\Phi [f_1 \star f_2] = \Phi [f_1]\Phi [f_2].\,</math>
where <math>\Phi</math> is the [[Wigner–Weyl transform]].

The star product is not commutative in general, but goes over to the ordinary commutative product of functions in the limit of  {{math|''ħ'' → 0}}. As such, it is said to define a [[Deformation theory|deformation]] of the commutative algebra of {{math|''C''<sup>∞</sup>(ℜ<sup>2</sup>)}}.

For the Weyl-map example above, the <small>★</small>-product may be written in terms of the [[Poisson bracket]] as
: <math>f_1 \star f_2 = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac {1}{n!} \left(\frac{i\hbar}{2} \right)^n  \Pi^n(f_1, f_2).</math>

Here,  Π is the [[Poisson manifold#The Poisson Bivector|Poisson bivector]], an operator defined such that its powers are
: <math>\Pi^0(f_1,f_2)=f_1f_2</math>
and
: <math>\Pi^1(f_1,f_2)=\{f_1,f_2\}= 
\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial q}
\frac{\partial f_2}{\partial p} -
\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial p}
\frac{\partial f_2}{\partial q} ~,
</math>
where {''f''<sub>1</sub>, ''f''<sub>2</sub>} is the [[Poisson bracket]]. More generally,
: <math>\Pi^n(f_1,f_2)=  \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k {n \choose k}
\left(
\frac{\partial^k }{\partial p^k}
\frac{\partial^{n-k}}{\partial q^{n-k}} f_1
\right) \times \left(
\frac{\partial^{n-k} }{\partial p^{n-k}}
\frac{\partial^k}{\partial q^k} f_2
\right) </math>
where <math>{n \choose k}</math> is the [[binomial coefficient]].

Thus, e.g.,<ref name="Zachos">
{{cite book
 |last3=Zachos |first3=C. K.
 |last2=Fairlie |first2=D. B.
 |last1=Curtright |first1=T. L.
 |year=2014
 |title=A Concise Treatise on Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space
 |publisher=[[World Scientific]]
 |isbn=9789814520430
}}
</ref> Gaussians compose [[Hyperbolic function#Comparison with circular trigonometric functions|hyperbolically]],
: <math>
\exp \left (-{a } (q^2+p^2)\right ) ~ \star ~
\exp \left (-{b} (q^2+p^2)\right ) = {1\over 1+\hbar^2 ab}
\exp \left (-{a+b\over 1+\hbar^2 ab} (q^2+p^2)\right ) ,
</math>
or
: <math>
 \delta (q) ~ \star ~ \delta(p) = {2\over h}
\exp \left (2i{qp\over\hbar}\right ) ,
</math>
etc.
These formulas are predicated on coordinates in which the [[Poisson bivector]] is constant (plain flat Poisson brackets). For the general formula on arbitrary [[Poisson manifold]]s, cf. the [[Kontsevich quantization formula]].

Antisymmetrization of this <small>★</small>-product yields the [[Moyal bracket]], the proper quantum deformation of the [[Poisson bracket]], and the phase-space isomorph (Wigner transform) of the quantum [[commutator]] in the more usual Hilbert-space formulation of quantum mechanics. As such, it provides the cornerstone of the dynamical equations of observables in this phase-space formulation.

There results a complete [[phase space formulation]] of quantum mechanics, '''''completely equivalent to the Hilbert-space operator representation''''', with star-multiplications paralleling operator multiplications isomorphically.<ref name="Zachos" />

Expectation values in phase-space quantization are obtained isomorphically to tracing operator observables {{mvar|Φ}} with the density matrix in Hilbert space:  they are obtained by phase-space integrals of observables such as the above {{mvar|f}} with the [[Wigner quasi-probability distribution]] effectively serving as a measure.

Thus, by expressing quantum mechanics in phase space (the same ambit as for classical mechanics), the above Weyl map facilitates recognition of quantum mechanics as a [[Deformation theory|deformation]] (generalization, cf. [[correspondence principle]]) of classical mechanics, with deformation parameter {{math|''ħ''/''S''}}.  (Other familiar deformations in physics involve the deformation of classical Newtonian into relativistic mechanics, with deformation parameter ''v''/''c''; or the deformation of Newtonian gravity into General Relativity, with deformation parameter Schwarzschild-radius/characteristic-dimension. Conversely, [[group contraction]] leads to the vanishing-parameter undeformed theories—[[classical limit]]s.)

Classical expressions, observables,  and operations (such as Poisson brackets) are modified by {{mvar|ħ}}-dependent quantum corrections, as the conventional commutative multiplication applying in classical mechanics is generalized to the ''noncommutative star-multiplication'' characterizing quantum mechanics and underlying its uncertainty principle.
